## Whole-object manipulation actions on boxes/parcels/totes — ranked head (warehouse/logistics robotics + OR)

**The dominant whole-object action set** (synthesized across Amazon Robotics, the Amazon Picking Challenge, and MHI material-handling taxonomy):

**1. MOVE / TRANSPORT (most frequent by far).** In the MHI taxonomy, "movement" is the first of the four core functions (movement, storage, protection, control), and unit-load transport equipment is the largest category. In order-picking OR, **travel/move dominates the time budget: ~55% of order-picking time is travel**, vs. searching 15%, extracting/grasping 10%, paperwork 20% (commonly cited OR figures). Picking itself is **50–55% of total warehouse operating cost**. Amazon's transport fleet (Hercules/Titan drive units, Pegasus, Proteus) exists purely to move totes/pods/carts — the single most-deployed robot class. Amazon reports ~**5 billion packages picked/stowed/packed/year (>13M/day)**, every one of which is moved/transported multiple times.

**2. PICK-AND-PLACE (pick + place + stow).** The canonical APC task: robots "pick items from shelves and place them into a tote" (Pick task) and "pick items from a tote and stow them into a shelf" (Stow task), **12 items per run**. Amazon's arm robots are all pick-and-place: Sparrow "picks up and moves individual items into totes" (singulation, picks **~65%** of inventory); Cardinal "picks, reads the label, and places into the appropriate cart" (up to 50 lb); Vulcan/Robin pick-and-place/stow (Vulcan handles **~75%** of item types). APC 2016 top scores: Stow — Delft 214, NimbRo 186, MIT 164; Pick — Delft 105, PFN 105, NimbRo 97 (top-10 Pick scores rose 38% year-over-year).

**3. SORT / SINGULATE / INDUCT.** Robin "grabs packages from the conveyor and places them onto drive units" (package sortation, >1,000 Robin arms deployed); Cardinal sorts packages into carts. Sortation/singulation/induction is one of MHI's named equipment classes and a top robotic-arm application in parcel hubs.

**4. PALLETIZE / DE-PALLETIZE + STACK / UN-STACK.** Unit-load formation (palletizing/unitizing) is one of MHI's core taxonomy branches. Robotic (mixed-case) palletizing = stacking boxes into stable pallets, ~300–2,200 cases/hour; depalletizing = un-stacking. Historically the last task to automate, now a fast-growing robotic segment. Stacking/un-stacking is the physical primitive underlying palletizing.

**5. REORIENT / FLIP (for barcode-facing or fit).** Lowest-frequency but explicitly present: in induction/sortation, parcels must be "oriented so barcodes can be read"; robots reorient parcels for label reading and rotate/orient boxes for pallet fit. Vendors note "five-sided in-motion barcode scanning to **reduce the need to reorient**" — i.e., reorient is a real, costly action they engineer around. APC pose-estimation/grasp-planning work also implies in-hand reorientation for fit.

### Numbers worth quoting
- Travel/move **55%** of pick time; search 15%, extract/grasp 10%, other 20%. Picking = **50–55%** of warehouse cost.
- Amazon: **~5B packages/yr (>13M/day)**; Sparrow picks **65%** of items; Vulcan **~75%** of item types; **>1,000** Robin arms.
- APC = **12 items**/run, two tasks (Pick, Stow). APC 2016: Stow Delft 214 / NimbRo 186 / MIT 164; Pick Delft 105 / PFN 105.
- MHI four functions: **movement, storage, protection, control**; unit-load = pallets/containers/totes.

### One-line takeaway
**Yes — MOVE/transport is the single most common whole-object action (it dominates time and the largest robot fleet), pick-and-place is the canonical second, and STACK (via palletizing) ranks among the most common; FLIP/REORIENT is genuinely present but the lowest-frequency of the head set — used mainly for barcode-facing and pallet-fit, and actively engineered around (five-sided in-motion scanning) rather than maximized.**

### Sources

- Amazon Sparrow (singulation, picks 65% of inventory): https://www.aboutamazon.com/news/operations/amazon-introduces-sparrow-a-state-of-the-art-robot-that-handles-millions-of-diverse-products

# Whole-Object Handling Actions on Manufacturing / Assembly Lines

## Ranked head of whole-object manipulation actions

**1. MOVE / TRANSPORT / PICK-PLACE (transfer between locations & stations)** — the single most common whole-object action by every taxonomy.
- **Therbligs (Gilbreth):** the object-displacement therbligs are *Transport Empty (TE)*, *Transport Loaded (TL)*, and *Grasp (G)* — these are the core "move the whole object" elements, distinct from in-place therbligs (assemble, position, use, hold). [Wikipedia – Therblig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Therblig)
- **MTM-1** distills the 18 therbligs into ~13 basic elements; the two transport elements are **Reach (R)** = move empty hand to object, and **Move (M)** = move object to a destination — the explicit whole-object displacement primitives, plus **Grasp (G)** and **Release (RL)** that bracket them. [Methods-time measurement – Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methods-time_measurement) / [MTM motion elements](https://www.yourarticlelibrary.com/ergonomics/work-measurement/9-basic-motion-elements-of-method-time-measurement/34568)
- **Robotics:** every industrial-skill survey ranks **pick-and-place** as the dominant primitive: "the most investigated robots' capabilities are pick and place" and "the placement-pick group is the most investigated." [Capability-based Frameworks for Industrial Robot Skills (arXiv 2203.00538)](https://arxiv.org/html/2203.00538v4)
- **Industry data (IFR World Robotics):** **Handling / machine tending ≈ 45%** of the global operational robot stock — the #1 application, ahead of welding/soldering (21%) and assembling/disassembling (11%). [IFR World Robotics – Industrial Robots Executive Summary](https://ifr.org/img/worldrobotics/Executive_Summary_WR_2024_Industrial_Robots.pdf) / [IFR press release](https://ifr.org/ifr-press-releases/news/global-robot-demand-in-factories-doubles-over-10-years). Within material handling, palletization/packaging is cited at ~83% of handling use cases. [AIPRM robotics statistics](https://www.aiprm.com/robotics-statistics/)

**2. ORIENT / FEED (part feeding + bringing to correct pose for the next op)** — pervasive because parts arrive in random pose.
- "The handling, orienting and feeding of parts as they arrive from vendors… must be done prior to robotic assembly since all such parts require reorienting for the assembly robot." [NIST Survey of Industrial Manipulation](https://tsapps.nist.gov/publication/get_pdf.cfm?pub_id=908608)
- The **vibratory bowl feeder** is named "the most common method for orienting parts," using a helical track + baffles to filter every pose but the target one. [Bowl feeder – Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowl_feeder)
- In DFA, this is captured by the **alpha (α) / beta (β) symmetry** angles — the rotations needed to bring a part to its insertion orientation — which directly drive handling time. [Boothroyd–Dewhurst DFA method](https://1library.net/article/boothroyd-dewhurst-dfa-method-design-for-assembly.yd2oe71q)

**3. REORIENT / FLIP / TURN-OVER (rotate whole object for the next operation)** — explicitly tracked as its own cost axis.
- **Therblig/MTM:** *Turn (T)* is a dedicated basic element. [MTM elements](https://www.yourarticlelibrary.com/ergonomics/work-measurement/9-basic-motion-elements-of-method-time-measurement/34568)
- **DFA "golden rules":** rule #6 is literally **"Minimize the need for re-orientations during assembly,"** and guidelines say to "avoid the need for rotation, releasing, and re-gripping" — DFA assigns explicit **time penalties for reorientation**. [Product design for manufacture and assembly, Boothroyd (1994)](http://static.sapucaia.ifsul.edu.br/professores/debarbajr/01.Fundamentos%20de%20Projeto/Artigos/14%20-%20DfMA%20-%20Product%20design%20for%20manufacture%20and%20assembly%20(1994).pdf)
- **Process example:** "quarter panels are formed in a press and are then removed, **inverted**, and inserted into a trimming press" — flip-for-next-operation is a canonical line motion. [Method for flipping a tray of parts (US 6,139,243)](https://image-ppubs.uspto.gov/dirsearch-public/print/downloadPdf/6139243)
- Modern manufacturability metrics (sheet-metal bending) quantify a **"part flip indicator," reorientation angle, and reorientation distance** between successive ops. [BenDFM taxonomy (arXiv 2603.13102)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.13102)

**4. FIXTURE / PLACE / POSITION (set the whole object into a jig/nest/location)** — bracketed with Position/Pre-position therbligs and the "Position (P)" MTM element; pick-and-place inherently ends in a place/seat action. [Parts Positioning – ASSEMBLY magazine](https://www.assemblymag.com/articles/82738-parts-positioning-fine-tuning-parts-placement)

**5. STACK / PALLETIZE / TRANSFER-BETWEEN-STATIONS** — the highest-volume *industrial* whole-object action class.
- Palletizing/packaging is the largest single handling deployment (~83% of handling robot use cited), and handling robots overall are 45% of stock; stacking/palletizing and inter-station transfer are explicitly the dominant material-handling use cases. [IFR Executive Summary](https://ifr.org/img/worldrobotics/Executive_Summary_WR_2024_Industrial_Robots.pdf) / [AIPRM](https://www.aiprm.com/robotics-statistics/) / [Industrial robot – Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Industrial_robot)

## Which whole-object motions recur most
Across all four source families the recurring head is: **(1) MOVE/transport (pick-and-place), (2) ORIENT/feed, (3) REORIENT/FLIP/turn, (4) FIXTURE/place, (5) STACK/palletize/transfer.**

## One-line takeaway
**Yes — MOVE (transport / pick-and-place), FLIP/REORIENT (Gilbreth "Turn," MTM "Turn," DFA's explicitly-penalized re-orientation), and STACK (palletize / transfer between stations) all rank among the most common whole-object actions:** MOVE is #1 in every taxonomy (handling ≈45% of installed robots; pick-and-place the top robotics primitive), STACK/palletize is the dominant industrial handling sub-class, and FLIP/REORIENT is universal enough that DFA's golden rules and MTM both make it a first-class, separately-costed motion.

# Whole-object REORIENTATION as a fundamental manipulation primitive — findings

## Is reorientation framed as a core/fundamental primitive? Yes — consistently.

- **In-hand reorientation = "a fundamental skill."** "In-hand reorientation is a fundamental skill in daily life and exemplifies the complexity of dexterous manipulation." — *From Simple to Complex Skills: The Case of In-Hand Object Reorientation* (arXiv 2501.05439). https://arxiv.org/html/2501.05439v1
- **Reorientation is the canonical/benchmark dexterous task.** OpenAI's Shadow Hand work uses **block (cube) reorientation to an arbitrary target orientation** as *the* benchmark in-hand task; episodes terminate at **50 consecutive successes** (the cap), and ADR policies later solved the Rubik's Cube. — *Learning Dexterous In-Hand Manipulation* (arXiv 1808.00177) https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.00177 ; *Solving Rubik's Cube with a Robot Hand* (arXiv 1910.07113) https://arxiv.org/pdf/1910.07113
- **Reorientation pairs with pick-place as complementary core operations.** "For complex manipulation scenarios where there are no common grasps, reorientation becomes mandatory… the object [is] reoriented to an intermediate pose and regrasped." Reorientation is what makes pick-and-place reach arbitrary SE(3) target poses. — ReorientDiff / AE-Reorient / ReorientBot (arXiv 2303.12700, 2202.11092). https://arxiv.org/pdf/2202.11092
- **Pivoting/tumbling/regrasping are the named reorientation primitives.** CMU work introduces **two motion primitives — pivot-on-support and roll-on-support** — and notes they "can solve more reorienting problems with fewer making and breaking contacts… compared to traditional pick-and-place based methods." Large-object planners "combine three manipulation styles: pivoting, tumbling, and regrasping." — *Reorienting Objects in 3D Space Using Pivoting* (arXiv 1912.02752) https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.02752 ; CMU "Fast Planning for 3D Any-Pose-Reorienting using Pivoting" https://www.ri.cmu.edu/app/uploads/2018/03/ICRA2018_Reorienting_by_Pivoting.pdf

## Is flip/turn-over near-universal across rigid objects? Effectively yes (as a capability target), with caveats.

- Pivoting is defined over objects of **"arbitrary known shape,"** i.e. applies broadly to rigid objects (arXiv 1912.02752).
- **Visual Dexterity** trained a *single* controller to reorient **150 objects to arbitrary target orientation in sim**, generalizing to novel real shapes — explicitly "**any rotation**" / full SO(3) reorientation as the goal. On a hard novel duck shape: dropped in **56%** of trials; when not dropped, reoriented within **0.4 rad (23°) 75%** of the time; **median ~7 s**. — *Visual Dexterity* (arXiv 2211.11744 / Science Robotics adc9244). https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.11744
- The same paper trained over **150 objects with one policy**, and *From Simple to Complex* reports real-world reorientation across 6 objects at **37.5%–93.3%** success (sim **88.25% ± 1.28** small-noise) — so reorientation is pursued as an object-general (near-universal-target) skill, even though *reliability* still varies by shape.
- **Why it's structurally necessary, not optional:** "pick-and-place alone cannot achieve arbitrary orientations in a single manipulation step, which is why regrasping becomes necessary… such as when flipping objects" — regrasp/in-hand literature. https://arxiv.org/pdf/2401.07915

## Ranked head of whole-object manipulation actions (synthesized across these sources)

1. **PICK-AND-PLACE / MOVE (translate-and-place)** — repeatedly called "a core robotic manipulation task" and "the most common method," the default prehensile primitive (arXiv 2310.00167, 2504.19502).
2. **REORIENT / FLIP / PIVOT / TUMBLE (change object orientation, incl. regrasping & in-hand)** — the second core whole-object primitive; "mandatory" whenever the target pose isn't directly graspable (1912.02752, 2303.12700, 1808.00177, 2211.11744).
3. **PUSH / SLIDE (non-prehensile translate)** — dominant for large/heavy objects where lifting is impractical (arXiv 2310.00167, "A Survey on Robot Pushing" PMC7805815).
4. **TOPPLE / TUMBLE / DRAG** — used in messy-tabletop rearrangement alongside the above (arXiv 2310.00167).
5. **STACK** — appears as a composite goal of pick-and-place (place-on-top) and in multi-layer rearrangement (arXiv 2306.14251), not as a distinct low-level primitive.

## One-line takeaway

Across this literature, **MOVE (pick-and-place/push) and FLIP/REORIENT are unambiguously the two most common, fundamental whole-object primitives** — pick-place handles position and reorient handles arbitrary SE(3) orientation (flip/turn-over treated as a near-universal target across rigid objects, achievable via pivoting/tumbling/regrasping/in-hand), whereas **STACK ranks lower as a composite goal built from pick-and-place rather than a primitive in its own right.**

# Whole-object transport-and-reorient vs in-place: how the taxonomies rank them

## 1. RT-1 (Robotics Transformer-1, Google 2022) — training skill set with instruction counts
RT-1's **Table 1** breaks its 744 instructions into a small skill set. Ranked by instruction count, the head is dominated by **whole-object transport**:

| Skill | # instructions | Type |
|---|---|---|
| **Move Object Near Object** | **337** | whole-object transport ("Move the first object near the second") |
| **Pick Object** | **130** | whole-object transport ("Lift the object off the surface") |
| **Pick from Receptacle and Place on Counter** | **162** | whole-object transport |
| **Place Object into Receptacle** | **84** | whole-object transport |
| Place Object Upright | 8 | **reorient** ("Place an elongated object upright") |
| Knock Object Over | 8 | reorient (inverse) |
| Open / Close Drawer | 3 / 3 | articulated, in-place |

> "the current set of skills includes picking, placing, opening and closing drawers, getting items in and out drawers, **placing elongated items up-right, knocking them over**..."

Takeaway from RT-1: the four largest skills (Move-near 337, Place-into-receptacle-pick 162, Pick 130, Place-into-receptacle 84) are **all whole-object transport**; reorient ("place upright"/"knock over") exists but is tiny (8 each). Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2212.06817 and https://robotics-transformer1.github.io/

## 2. RT-2 (2023) — inherits RT-1's verb set
RT-2 keeps the same low-level action grammar (pick / move / place) and adds **emergent** capability categories (symbol understanding, reasoning, human recognition), e.g. "move apple to 3", "move coke can to person with glasses", "pick up the smallest object." Whole-object **move/pick/place** remain the action backbone; the novelty is semantic grounding, not new primitive verbs. Source: https://robotics-transformer2.github.io/ , https://arxiv.org/pdf/2307.15818

## 3. BEHAVIOR-1K (Stanford, 1,000 activities)
Long-horizon activities are executed via a small set of **action primitives**: 
> abstractions such as **"pick," "place," "push," "navigate," "dip," "wipe."**

Here **pick / place** (whole-object transport) and **push** (non-prehensile move) are the manipulation primitives; the rest are locomotion (navigate) or in-place tool actions (dip, wipe). Source: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2403.09227

## 4. Gilbreth therbligs (motion-study, 1910s) — 18 elements, with an explicit transport vs in-place split
The canonical list: Search, Find, Select, **Grasp**, **Position**, **Assemble**, Use, Disassemble, Inspect, **Transport Loaded**, Pre-position, **Release Load**, **Transport Empty**, Unavoidable Delay, Avoidable Delay, Rest, Plan, Hold.

This is the **original "transport vs in-place" distinction**:
- **Transport Loaded (TL)** = "moving an object using a hand motion" — the whole-object move, classed **effective/value-adding**.
- **Position (P)** = "orienting an object in the defined location" — the **in-place reorient**, classed **ineffective** (a fine-adjustment cost to be minimized).
- Transport Empty (TE), the empty return reach, is effective-but-to-be-minimized.

So therbligs already rank whole-object **Transport** as the productive core, with in-place **Position** (reorient) treated as overhead to reduce. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Therblig , https://web.mit.edu/allanmc/www/Therblgs.pdf

## 5. Wörgötter et al., "A Simple Ontology of Manipulation Actions based on Hand–Object Relations" (IEEE TAMD, 2013)
A tree-structured ontology built from touch/un-touch temporal anchors, yielding **"less than 30 basic actions with three associated manipulation types and six goal categories."** Named members include **Putting, Taking (pick-and-place), Pushing, Hiding, Uncovering, Stirring, Cutting, Chopping.** The top split is between **separation** vs **release-/merge-determined** actions — i.e., whole-object **Putting/Taking/pick-and-place and Pushing** sit alongside in-place operations (stir/cut/chop) in one compact set. Source: https://iis.uibk.ac.at/public/papers/Worgotter-2013-TAMD.pdf , https://dl.acm.org/doi/abs/10.1109/TAMD.2012.2232291

## 6. Prehensile vs non-prehensile (the modern "transport" axis)
The recurring canonical primitive set in robot-learning surveys is **{pick, place, push}**: 
> "The manipulation primitives most commonly used are {push, pick, place}."

Pick/place = prehensile whole-object transport; push = non-prehensile whole-object move; stacking = repeated place-on-top. Source: https://arxiv.org/pdf/1901.03557 , https://arxiv.org/html/2512.11080 , https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7805815/ (push survey)

---

## Ranked head of whole-object manipulation actions (synthesis across sources)
1. **PICK** — universal; therblig Grasp+Transport-Loaded, RT-1 (130) "Pick Object", BEHAVIOR pick, Wörgötter "Taking", canonical {pick,place,push}.
2. **PLACE / put-down** — universal; RT-1 place-into-receptacle (84) + pick-place-on-counter (162), BEHAVIOR place, Wörgötter "Putting".
3. **MOVE (transport A→B)** — RT-1's single **largest** skill, "Move Object Near Object" = **337** instructions; therblig **Transport Loaded** (effective core); push as non-prehensile move in BEHAVIOR/Wörgötter and the {pick,place,**push**} set.
4. **PUSH** — explicit primitive in BEHAVIOR-1K, Wörgötter, and the canonical {push,pick,place}; non-prehensile whole-object transport.
5. **STACK / put-on-top** — recurring as a derived whole-object action (place-on-object); appears as "put on top" in Wörgötter's putting family; standard benchmark task but not usually its own top-level verb (it's a constrained Place).
6. **FLIP / REORIENT** — present but **lower-ranked / treated as overhead**: RT-1 "Place Upright"/"Knock Over" (8 each); therblig **Position** is explicitly classed **ineffective**. Reorientation is acknowledged as a distinct hard sub-problem but is rarely in the top-frequency head.

## One-line takeaway
**MOVE and PUSH are unambiguously among the most common whole-object actions** (move is literally RT-1's #1 skill at 337; push is in every canonical {pick,place,push} set), and **STACK** appears as a frequent derived place-on-top action — but **FLIP/REORIENT is the outlier**: across RT-1 (8 instr.) and the Gilbreth therbligs (Position = "ineffective"), whole-object reorientation is treated as a small, lower-frequency, overhead-like operation rather than part of the high-frequency transport core.

Sources: [RT-1 paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.06817) · [RT-1 site](https://robotics-transformer1.github.io/) · [RT-2](https://robotics-transformer2.github.io/) · [BEHAVIOR-1K](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2403.09227) · [Therblig (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Therblig) · [Gilbreth therbligs (MIT)](https://web.mit.edu/allanmc/www/Therblgs.pdf) · [Wörgötter 2013 ontology](https://iis.uibk.ac.at/public/papers/Worgotter-2013-TAMD.pdf) · [non-prehensile rearrangement](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1901.03557) · [non-prehensile taxonomy 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2512.11080) · [robot pushing survey](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7805815/)

# Whole-object two-handed actions: ranked evidence from ergonomics + bimanual benchmarks

## Ergonomics / manual materials handling (MMH)

- **NIOSH Revised Lifting Equation (RNLE)** is, by definition, an analysis of *two-handed* whole-object handling: "calculates the risk for back injuries from **two-handed lifting tasks**" performed by one person standing; defined as "manually grasping an object **with two hands** and vertically moving the object." Load Constant **LC = 51 lb (≈23 kg)** under ideal conditions; recommended Lifting Index ≤ 1.0. So in the canonical industrial standard, the default *unit action* on a medium/large object is inherently two-handed. ([CDC RNLE](https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/ergonomics/about/RNLE.html), [ergo-plus](https://ergo-plus.com/niosh-lifting-equation-single-task/))
- The core MMH activity set in the NIOSH framework is **lift / lower / carry / push / pull / hold** — i.e., MOVE-class actions dominate the taxonomy of whole-object handling. ([VelocityEHS](https://www.ehs.com/blogs/a-how-to-guide-the-niosh-lifting-equation/))
- **Two-person / team carry** is the standard escalation when one person + two hands is insufficient (heavy/large objects), confirming carry/transport as the prototypical whole-object action: two-person *carrying* efficiency ≈ **96.2%** of one-person method; team *lifting* capacity is greater than one person but **10–20% below** the summed individual capacity; boxes *with handles* raise max acceptable carry weight. ([ScienceDirect](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0169814101000336), [Ergoweb](https://ergoweb.com/two-person-lift-team/), [Sharp et al. 1995](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/154193129503901021))

## Bimanual manipulation benchmarks

- **PerAct2** (13 tasks / 23 variations; classified by Krebs et al. taxonomy on coordination + *physical coupling* = one arm exerts force the other can measure). The **"coupled" single-whole-object** tasks are: **Push box, Lift a ball, Pick up a plate, Lift tray** (plus Straighten rope, deformable). So the genuinely-two-handed whole-object set is dominated by **MOVE (lift/carry/push)** verbs. ([PerAct2 arXiv](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.00278v1), [bimanual.github.io](https://bimanual.github.io/))
- **BiManiBench** coordination taxonomy names **"Synchronous Collaborative Manipulation = both arms actuate simultaneously on a single shared object (e.g., dual-arm lifting)"** as the core whole-object mode; high-level action set = pick, place, **stack**, handover, rotate. ([BiManiBench arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.08392))
- **Krebs et al. bimanual taxonomy** (the classifier both benchmarks use): same-object two-handed categories are **carry/transport/hold, lift, flip/turn-over, rotate/reorient, stack/place**, organized by coordinated-vs-uncoordinated, tightly-vs-loosely coupled, symmetric-vs-asymmetric (symmetric two-handed lift = canonical tightly-coupled case). ([Krebs2022 PDF](https://h2t.iar.kit.edu/pdf/Krebs2022.pdf))

## Ranked head of genuinely two-handed whole-object actions (by cross-source prevalence)

1. **Two-hand carry / transport / lift (MOVE)** — most common; it is the *defining* unit of NIOSH MMH, the two-person escalation case, and the largest coupled-task group in PerAct2/BiManiBench ("dual-arm lifting").
2. **Two-hand push of a heavy/large item** — explicit in MMH (push/pull) and PerAct2 "Push box."
3. **Two-hand stack / place** — named primitive in BiManiBench's high-level set; standard end-of-transport action.
4. **Two-hand rotate-to-inspect / reorient** — present as a category (Krebs, BiManiBench "rotate") but lower-frequency than move/place.
5. **Two-hand flip / turn-over of a box** — genuinely two-handed and in the Krebs taxonomy, but the *least* represented as a named task in the robotics benchmarks (more implied than enumerated).

## Takeaway
**MOVE (two-hand carry/lift/push) is unambiguously the single most common whole-object two-handed action across both ergonomics and robotics sources; STACK/PLACE is consistently in the head as the standard terminal action; FLIP/REORIENT are genuine but secondary** — well-attested as categories, yet ranked below move and place in task frequency.

## (2) Recommendation: ADD FLIP/REORIENT as the third universal inter task; do NOT add STACK

### ADD **FLIP / REORIENT** — yes, as universal inter task #3.

**Why it earns the universal floor (the principled bar = "canonical, self-contained, whole-object primitive that exists on essentially any rigid object"):**
- It is the **second fundamental whole-object primitive** alongside transport in the robotics-manipulation literature — pick-place handles *position*, reorient handles *orientation*; together they span SE(3). Three of your five angles (reorient/regrasp, manufacturing-line, warehouse-logistics) independently rank it in the head set.
- It is **self-contained**: turning an object over / rotating it to inspect needs only the object itself — no second object, no surface, no environment. This is the same self-containment test that PICK UP and MOVE pass, and that STACK fails.
- It is **near-universal across rigid objects** as a capability target ("any rotation" over 150 objects; pivoting defined for "arbitrary known shape"), so like pick-up it applies to every object as a valid two-region grounding target.
- It **fills a real gap**: your current set has TRANSPORT (pick-up, move) but no RECONFIGURE axis. Logistics/production explicitly study flip/reorient as a named, separately-costed action (DFA penalty, barcode-facing, pallet-fit) — exactly the domains the user wants the set grounded in.

**Caveat to honor in the writeup (do not oversell):** the count-based taxonomies (RT-1, therbligs) rank reorient as *lower-frequency overhead*, not a top-of-head action. So frame it as "the canonical RECONFIGURE primitive that completes the whole-object axis", **not** as "as common as move". This keeps the claim defensible.

**Crucial design fit — it is NOT a new coordination scheme.** Your locked taxonomy already absorbs it: **scheme B (co-support) sub-mode `:reorient`** (locked refinement #2, "relabel scheme B so flips = rotate+rotate on body aren't mislabeled as carry"). So FLIP/REORIENT enters the universal set **without touching the 3-scheme taxonomy or the core-9 role set** — it reuses `rotate` (already axis-parameterized to absorb tilt/flip) and `support`/`lift`. This is the cleanest possible addition: a new *task*, zero new *primitives*.

### Is FLIP/REORIENT genuinely two-handed only for medium/large? — **YES. Size-gate it exactly like MOVE.**

The bimanual NECESSITY of flip is **force/leverage-driven, not orientation-driven**, which is precisely the size axis:
- **Small object** (one-hand graspable): you flip it *in-hand* by re-grasping/wrist-rotation — a one-handed dexterous action (the in-hand reorientation literature is explicitly single-hand: OpenAI Shadow Hand, Visual Dexterity = one hand/one controller). → Genuinely bimanual = **NO**. Treat like the one-hand pick-up case: accept the W2 "not-truly-bimanual" flag, keep it as a valid asymmetric two-region grounding target (one hand rotates, other steadies), do **not** manufacture a fake stabilizer.
- **Medium object** (two-handed-size, e.g. a box/crate): you must grip **two opposing edges/faces** to generate the couple (torque) that rotates it — no single grasp gives enough leverage. → Genuinely bimanual = **YES**. This is the scheme-B `:reorient` parallel-torque case.
- **Large/furniture object** (too heavy to lift): you don't flip free-space — you **tip/pivot/tumble about a bottom edge** that stays on the ground (the pivot-on-support / roll-on-support / tumbling primitives from CMU). One hand pulls/rotates at the top, the other supports/guides — still two-handed. → Genuinely bimanual = **YES**, but a different role split (see below).

So the **same size-gate you already use for MOVE** (one-hand / two-handed-size = carry / furniture = push-roll) maps cleanly onto FLIP (in-hand / two-edge-couple / tip-pivot). Reuse the gate verbatim.

**STACK fails the self-containment test that defines the universal set.** Stacking *requires a second object or a target surface/pallet* ("place-on-top of another object"). Per your own locked principle, the universal floor holds only **self-contained whole-object tasks** (pick-up, move, flip) where both regions are on the *one* object being annotated. **Same exclusion logic, for the record, applies to PLACE-into-receptacle, INSERT-into-hole, POUR** — all need a second entity/target and stay out of the universal floor.
